question: A 37-year-old male presents to general medical clinic reporting sleeping difficulties. He states that he has daytime sleepiness, having fallen asleep several times while driving his car recently. He sometimes experiences very vivid dreams just before awakening. You ask the patient's wife if she has witnessed any episodes where her husband lost all muscle tone and fell to the ground, and she confirms that he has not had this symptom. The patient notes that this condition runs in his family, and he desperately asks for treatment. You begin him on a first-line medication for this illness, which works by which mechanism of action?

options.opb: Agonist at the mu opioid receptor

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Sleep difficulties -> Daytime sleepiness -> Falling asleep while driving -> Vivid dreams before awakening -> No episodes of muscle tone loss -> Family history of the condition -> First-line medication initiation -> Mechanism of action understanding -> Alpha-2 receptor antagonist -> 95%
analysis: The patient's symptoms of daytime sleepiness, vivid dreams, and episodes of muscle tone loss without falling are suggestive of narcolepsy. The first-line medication for narcolepsy is typically a stimulant medication to help with excessive daytime sleepiness. Stimulant medications work by enhancing the release of norepinephrine and dopamine in the brain to promote wakefulness.
